visibleText: D Product Security OS DestroSolutions Home Products Friday Inbox Chats Projects Run history Security Vulnerabilities Threat intel PSIRT Supply chain Compliance Workspace Reports Integrations Settings Search products, CVEs, playbooks… Ctrl K SS Singh Admin LEARN Overview Documents OPERATE SBOM Builder License risk Container scan Destro Gate Renovate bridge Early signals OSS steward REFERENCE Articles (71) Annexes (8) Standards Timeline RASIC Open source ENISA SRP Compliance dashboard REFERENCE · REGULATION (EU) 2024/2847 OSV · < 15m · 99.5% SLO Understand the Cyber Resilience Act The path to conformity, your obligations by role, how CE marking works, and the dates that matter — each tied to its Article or Annex. Run the assessments from the Compliance dashboard. THE PROBLEM Connected products shipped with weak defaults, no patches, and no one accountable across their lifecycle. National rules were patchy and voluntary. WHAT IT DOES Makes cybersecurity a mandatory product requirement EU-wide — security by design, vulnerability handling, a guaranteed support period — enforced with CE marking. WHO IT COVERS Any product with digital elements made available on the EU market. Duties fall on manufacturers, importers, distributors and open-source stewards. Application timeline · Article 71 Full timeline 11 Dec 2024 Entry into force 11 Jun 2026 Conformity bodies notified 11 Sep 2026 Reporting obligations apply 11 Dec 2027 Full application The path to conformity Five steps · each opens its tool 1 Classify the product Art 7 · Annex III / IV Tick the core-function categories. Highest class wins — Default, Important I/II, Critical. The class sets the conformity route. Scope & classification 2 Assess risk, meet Annex I Art 13(2) · Annex I Part I Run the risk assessment and meet the essential requirements — secure-by-default, encryption, access control, attack-surface reduction. Gap analysis 3 Stand up vulnerability handling Annex I Part II · Art 14 Machine-readable SBOM, a published CVD policy, free security updates, and the 24h / 72h / 14d ENISA reporting pipeline. Compliance checklist 4 Assemble the technical file + DoC Annex VII · Annex V Architecture, SBOM, risk assessment, test reports and the EU Declaration of Conformity — retained 10 years (Art 13(13)). Document templates 5 Conformity assessment → CE Art 32 · Art 30 Run the assessment route for the class, affix the CE marking, and file the self-assessment and evidence pack. Self-assessment Your obligations by role Supply-chain RACI Manufacturer Article 13 Designs or produces a product with digital elements and markets it under their name. ▸ Meet the Annex I essential requirements on a risk assessment — Art 13(2)–(4). ▸ Determine and disclose a support period ≥ 5 years — Art 13(8). ▸ Keep technical documentation 10 years — Annex VII · Art 13(13). ▸ Draw up the EU Declaration of Conformity and affix CE — Art 28 · 30. ▸ Report exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents — Art 14. Importer Article 17 Established in the Union and places a product bearing a non-EU person's name or trademark on the market. ▸ Place only products that meet the essential requirements — Art 17. ▸ Verify the manufacturer ran the conformity assessment, drew up technical docs, affixed CE and supplied the Annex II information. ▸ Do not place a product known, or with reason to be believed, non-compliant — and flag a contained vulnerability to the manufacturer. ▸ Put your name and contact address on the product or its packaging. Distributor Article 18 Anyone in the supply chain other than the manufacturer or importer who makes a product available on the market. ▸ Act with due care for the CRA requirements — Art 18. ▸ Before making available, verify the CE marking is affixed and the Annex II information is supplied. ▸ Do not make available a product known, or with reason to be believed, non-compliant. ▸ Keep storage and transport conditions from jeopardising compliance. Software / open-source steward Article 24 A legal person that systematically supports development of FOSS intended for commercial activity. ▸ Put in place a cybersecurity policy for secure development — Art 24(1). ▸ Cooperate with market surveillance authorities — Art 24(2). ▸ Report exploited vulnerabilities you become aware of — Art 24(3) → 14. ▸ Lighter regime — non-commercial contributors stay out of scope. CE marking under the CRA The CE marking is the manufacturer's declaration that the product meets the CRA essential requirements. It is affixed before the product is placed on the market (Art 30), backed by a completed conformity assessment (Art 32), the EU Declaration of Conformity (Art 28 · Annex V), and the technical documentation (Annex VII). For Important Class II and Critical products a notified body is involved, and its four-digit number sits next to the marking. PRODUCT CLASS CONFORMITY ASSESSMENT ROUTE BASIS Default Module A — internal control (self-assessment) Art 32(1) Important · Class I Module A if harmonised standards applied in full; otherwise B+C or H Art 32(2) Important · Class II Always third-party — Module B+C, Module H, or an EU certificate Art 32(3) Critical B+C / H, plus an EU cybersecurity certificate where a delegated act requires it Art 32(4) Check your class Declaration of Conformity template What you must do Secure by design Annex I Part I Vulnerability handling + SBOM Annex I Part II Support period ≥ 5 years Art 13(8) CE marking + Declaration of Conformity Art 28 · 30 Incident reporting 24h / 72h / 14d Art 14 Technical documentation, 10-year retention Annex VII · Art 13(13) Article 64 penalties €15M / 2.5% Essential requirements · Art 13 · Art 14 €10M / 2% Procedural and conformity breaches €5M / 1% Misleading information to authorities Whichever is higher of the cap or the percentage of global turnover. Official guidance & further reading Primary sources European Commission — CRA Policy, FAQ and guidance ENISA — Cyber Resilience Act Technical guidance · SRP EUR-Lex — Regulation 2024/2847 The authoritative legal text Streamlex — CRA, article by article Clear, cross-referenced reading Reference library Verbatim Regulation + plain English 71 ITEMS Articles I – VIII Annexes MILESTONES Timeline ROLES RASIC STEWARDS Open source ISO / IEC Standards REPORTING ENISA SRP Documents required for CRA conformity 25 artifacts · 5 buckets Every artifact the CRA requires, grouped by purpose. Each row tells you the document, its Article or Annex reference, what kind of document it is, what existing artifact you can adapt, and the standards you can map an existing equivalent to — so a mature 27001 or 62443 programme doesn't start from zero. Technical file Annex VII Retained 10 years (Art 13(13)). Must be furnished to market-surveillance authorities on a reasoned request. Cover all 9 mandatory items in §1–§9. visibleText: D Product Security OS DestroSolutions Home Products Friday Inbox Chats Projects Run history Security Vulnerabilities Threat intel PSIRT Supply chain Compliance Workspace Reports Integrations Settings Search products, CVEs, playbooks… Ctrl K SS Singh Admin INTEGRATIONS CI/CD quick start Upload SBOMs from your pipeline 1 · Create an API key Give it the upload and read scopes. Open API keys 2 · Save it as a CI secret Name it DESTRO_API_KEY — GitHub: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions. GitLab: Settings → CI/CD → Variables (masked). 3 · Add the job Product name in DestroSolutions API address: https://iaxxugiyicroptkuhgyj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api-gateway GitHub Actions GitLab CI Save as .github/workflows/destrosolutions-sbom.yml name: DestroSolutions SBOM scan on: push: branches: [main] workflow_dispatch: jobs: sbom: runs-on: ubuntu-latest env: DESTRO_API: "https://iaxxugiyicroptkuhgyj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api-gateway" PRODUCT_NAME: "My product" PRODUCT_VERSION: ${{ github.ref_name }} steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v4 - name: Generate CycloneDX SBOM uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0 with: format: cyclonedx-json output-file: sbom.cdx.json - name: Upload SBOM and gate on critical findings env: DESTRO_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.DESTRO_API_KEY }} run: | set -eu q() { jq -rn --arg v "$1" '$v|@uri'; } curl -sS --fail-with-body -X POST \ "$DESTRO_API/api/v1/sbom/upload?product_name=$(q "$PRODUCT_NAME")&product_version=$(q "$PRODUCT_VERSION")&file_name=sbom.cdx.json" \ -H "X-API-Key: $DESTRO_API_KEY" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ --data-binary @sbom.cdx.json -o upload.json || { cat upload.json; echo; exit 1; } IMPORT_ID=$(jq -r .data.import_id upload.json) echo "Uploaded, scan $IMPORT_ID" for i in $(seq 1 60); do curl -sS --fail-with-body "$DESTRO_API/api/v1/scans/$IMPORT_ID" -H "X-API-Key: $DESTRO_API_KEY" -o scan.json || { cat scan.json; echo; exit 1; } [ "$(jq -r .data.finished scan.json)" = "true" ] && break sleep 10 done jq .data scan.json [ "$(jq -r .data.status scan.json)" = "completed" ] || { echo "Scan not completed"; exit 1; } CRITICAL=$(jq -r .data.product_findings_by_severity.critical scan.json) echo "Critical findings on this product: $CRITICAL" [ "$CRITICAL" -eq 0 ] Copy The job uploads the SBOM to the product version named after the branch or tag, waits for matching to finish, and fails when the product has critical findings. No royalty. Destro Scanner is a single Go binary that produces CycloneDX 1.6 SBOMs from your source tree, running OS, or container images. Apache-2.0 underneath, built on the same osv-scalibr engine OSV-Scanner ships. Run it in CI, pipe the output to our upload endpoint, and your CRA Annex I Part II §1 evidence is on file. Why we own it No partnership · no SaaS dependency LICENSE Apache-2.0 We can vendor, fork, and rebrand without licence fees or notice. ENGINE osv-scalibr Same Google library OSV-Scanner v2.0 ships — feature parity by construction. OUTPUT CycloneDX 1.6 The newest CDX revision, accepted by every downstream regulator and tool. RUNTIME Single Go binary Static binary, no Python / Node / Java runtime required. Ships in customer CI in seconds. TARGETS Linux · macOS · Windows Same binary set in every CI runner the customer already uses. PRIVACY On-prem by default Scans run on the customer's machine. We never see the source — only the resulting SBOM, on upload. Install Homebrew · Linux · Windows MACOS / HOMEBREW brew install destrosolutions/tap/destro LINUX (CURL) curl -sSfL https://destrosolutions.com/install.sh | sh CONTAINER docker run --rm -v $(pwd):/src ghcr.io/destrosolutions/scanner sbom repo /src Three scan modes 3 modes · one binary · CycloneDX out Source repository Parses every lockfile, manifest, and language file across npm, PyPI, Maven, Go, Cargo, NuGet, RubyGems, Packagist, Hex, and more — recursively, in one pass. destro sbom repo . → cyclonedx.json Running OS / firmware Detects installed OS packages (apk, dpkg, rpm), kernel build metadata, and firmware blobs on the running host. Useful for embedded products without a build manifest. destro sbom os → cyclonedx.json Container image Pull from a registry, load an OCI archive, or read the local Docker daemon. Per-layer attribution shows which Dockerfile line introduced each component. destro sbom container <image> → cyclonedx.json Upload to the platform Once you have the CycloneDX file, pipe it to our upload endpoint. The same SBOM ingestion pipeline that already powers /sbom consumes it — matched against OSV.dev's ~775k records, persisted as Annex I Part II §1 evidence, and surfaced in the CVE pipeline. destro sbom upload cyclonedx.json --product=<id> Open SBOM hub Add to PR gate Scan container instead Recent SBOM imports 4 imports tcu-200-4.2.1.cdx.json CYCLONEDX 3 comp 22/09/2026, 12:17:55 ivi-700-11.0.6.cdx.json CYCLONEDX 3 comp 24/09/2026, 12:17:55 bms-050-2.7.0.spdx.json SPDX 2 comp 28/09/2026, 12:17:55 evse-310-1.4.2.cdx.json CYCLONEDX 2 comp 12/10/2026, 12:17:55 How this maps to the CRA • Each scan run satisfies Annex I Part II §1 (machine-readable SBOM, ≥ top-level deps). • Per-layer container attribution becomes Annex VII §2 architecture-diagram evidence. • Detected components route through OSV.dev's matching, populating Annex VII §6 verification reports. • The signed scan timestamp + binary hash become append-only audit-trail rows (Art 13(13), 10-year retention). Provenance Destro Scanner is a downstream packaging of think-ahead-technologies/kunnus-scanner — Apache-2.0, vendored under our binary name with the upstream notice intact. The osv-scalibr engine and CycloneDX emitter are Google's, also Apache-2.0. We add the upload endpoint, the device-auth integration, and the platform evidence wiring; we do not relicense the scan engine or claim ownership of it. © 2026 DestroSolutions Friday Good afternoon, Singh. ⊟ 6 exploited CVEs are open. COMPLIANCE · LICENSE RISK License risk across your OSS dependencies Detects copyleft contamination, restrictive commercial clauses, and unlicensed code before they reach market. Powered by OSV-Scanner's license module — same scan pass as the vulnerability scanner, no extra cost. License families & CRA posture 5 families · posture · CRA impact FAMILY EXAMPLES POSTURE CRA IMPACT Permissive MIT · BSD-3-Clause · Apache-2.0 · ISC Generally ship-safe; require attribution. Low — Annex II §6 attribution applies. Weak copyleft LGPL-2.1 · LGPL-3.0 · MPL-2.0 · EPL-2.0 Linkable, but modifications to the library must be open. Medium — modifications must be disclosable to users. Strong copyleft GPL-2.0 · GPL-3.0 · AGPL-3.0 Combining with proprietary code triggers viral source-disclosure terms. High — review distribution model before market entry. Restrictive / commercial BUSL-1.1 · SSPL-1.0 · Elastic-2.0 Field-of-use restrictions; check competitive-use clauses. Variable — confirm allowed use cases. Unlicensed / unknown No license · Proprietary Treat as 'all rights reserved' — do not ship without resolution. Critical — blocks DoC + CE marking. Findings · DestroSolutions unavailable How the scan runs 1. Lockfile parsing Worker reads each product's manifest — package-lock.json, go.mod, pom.xml, Cargo.lock, requirements.txt, Pipfile.lock, etc. Identical input as the vuln scan. 2. Family resolution License strings normalise to one of the five families. Multi-license SPDX expressions (e.g. "MIT OR Apache-2.0") resolve to the safest applicable family for downstream selection. 3. CRA mapping Every flagged dependency surfaces as evidence on the Annex II §6 attribution checklist and the Annex VII technical file. Critical findings block CE marking until cleared. Block + audit If a new finding exceeds policy, merge is blocked and an immutable row lands in the audit ledger with the SARIF + the override signer (if any). Install on a repo Two options. INTEGRATIONS · RENOVATE & DEPENDABOT Your existing dependency-update bot, visible to PSIRT Renovate uses OSV.dev directly. Dependabot uses GitHub's advisory feed (an OSV upstream). Both already open PRs that fix vulnerabilities in your customers' repos — we just connect the dots so PSIRT and the CRA audit trail see the same flow. Lifecycle Four steps · zero customer code change 1 Renovate / Dependabot opens a PR Their bot already runs on the customer's repo. It detects a vulnerable dependency and creates a PR with the upgrade. 2 Webhook fires to /api/webhooks/renovate GitHub or GitLab sends the PR-creation event to our endpoint. Payload includes the PR body, which references the CVE / GHSA / OSV ID. 3 We mark the finding in-progress Match the referenced ID against `cve_findings`. Flip status to remediation_in_progress with the PR URL. Surfaces on PSIRT immediately. 4 PR merges → finding closes Merge webhook flips the finding to fixed. Audit-trail row records the actor, PR, commit SHA, and the OSV record that triggered the chain. Zero manual work. Works with the bot you already have Renovate (self-hosted or Mend.io). Dependabot. Whitesource bolt. Snyk. Any bot that opens PRs referencing CVE / GHSA / OSV IDs. One endpoint POST to /api/webhooks/renovate with the platform's standard pull_request event. We accept the GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket variants from the same URL. visibleText: D Product Security OS DestroSolutions Home Products Friday Inbox Chats Projects Run history Security Vulnerabilities Threat intel PSIRT Supply chain Compliance Workspace Reports Integrations Settings Search products, CVEs, playbooks… Ctrl K SS Singh Admin LEARN Overview Documents OPERATE SBOM Builder License risk Container scan Destro Gate Renovate bridge Early signals OSS steward REFERENCE Articles (71) Annexes (8) Standards Timeline RASIC Open source ENISA SRP Compliance dashboard COMPLIANCE · OSS STEWARD Steward platform for open-source maintainers CRA Article 24 introduces lighter-but-real duties for organisations that systematically support FOSS development for commercial activity. This is the end-to-end workflow: register, write your policy, publish vulnerability records to OSV.dev, route Article 14 reports to ENISA. What stewards must do Article 24 · three duties Art 24(1) Cybersecurity policy Document secure-development practices for the supported project. Maps to ISO/IEC 27034 application security and OWASP SAMM. Art 24(2) Cooperate with market surveillance Maintain a public contact, respond to authority requests, supply evidence of the cybersecurity policy on demand. Art 24(3) → Art 14 Report exploited vulnerabilities Stewards inherit the 24h / 72h / 14d reporting cadence for vulnerabilities they become aware of. Non-commercial individual contributors stay out of scope. Onboarding workflow Four steps · each persists evidence 1 Register the project Identify the steward legal entity, the OSS project(s) under stewardship, and the contact mailbox. We mint a stable steward ID used in CSAF and OSV records. 2 Draft the cybersecurity policy Start from the policy template — secure-coding rules, code-review gates, dependency policy, supply-chain controls. Versioned and retained for 10 years. 3 Publish to OSV via REST When a vulnerability is confirmed, push an OSV-format record to the public database via OSV's REST contribution endpoint. CURL joined the database this way in Feb 2024. 4 Route to ENISA SRP Same record fans out to the ENISA Single Reporting Platform with the Article 14 stage selected (early warning / notification / final report). Audit ledger retains the submission. OSV.dev contribution path New as of Feb 2024 — OSV.dev accepts vulnerability records via a REST contribution endpoint. We post on your behalf, attach the signed CSAF advisory as an alternative format, and surface the OSV ID + ENISA SRP confirmation in your audit ledger. The same record reaches downstream consumers (GitHub Advisory Database, RustSec, Renovate, Dependabot) within the OSV.dev 15-minute freshness SLO. OSV data sources ENISA SRP routing Cybersecurity policy template What stewards do NOT inherit • Conformity assessment + CE marking — stewards don't ship a CE-marked product; manufacturers downstream do. • Annex VII full technical documentation retention — they keep cybersecurity-policy evidence, not the manufacturer's complete file. • Annex V/VI Declaration of Conformity — manufacturers issue DoCs, not stewards. • Non-commercial individual maintainers stay fully out of scope under Recital 18 and Article 24. product with digital elements on the EU market APPLIES FROM 11 Dec 2027 · full application PENALTY Up to €15M / 2.5% THE central manufacturer article. 24 sub-paragraphs cover pre-market design + risk assessment, vulnerability handling, support period (≥5 years), technical documentation, user information, third-party component due diligence, and end-of-support communication. Article 13 is the workhorse — read this Article first if you read nothing else. It captures every continuing obligation the manufacturer owns from the moment they decide to ship the product to 10 years after the last unit is placed on the market. The sequence in practice: 1. Risk-assess the product (13(2)) and document the assessment. 2. Design against Annex I Part I (5) and put Annex I Part II processes in place. 3. Identify and remediate vulnerabilities in third-party components (13(5)-(6)), including FOSS. 4. Set a support period (13(8)) of at least 5 years (or shorter only if the product's expected lifetime is shorter). 5. Make security updates available during the support period (13(9)). 6. Draw up Annex VII technical documentation (13(10)) and keep it for 10 years. 7. Identify yourself on the product (13(14)-(15)). 8. Designate a public point of contact for vulnerability reports (13(16)). 9. Disclose fixed vulnerabilities publicly (13(20)). 10. Notify users at least 12 months before end of support (13(23)). Non-compliance with this Article sits in Penalty Tier 1 — €15M or 2.5% of global turnover. KEY OBLIGATIONS ▸ 24 sub-paragraphs; the manufacturer's central rulebook ▸ Support period: at least 5 years OR the expected lifetime, whichever is shorter (but never less than 5 unless lifetime really is shorter) ▸ Technical documentation must be retained 10 years after last placement ▸ End-of-support: 12-month minimum notice to users ▸ Tier 1 penalty: up to €15M or 2.5% of global turnover VERBATIM — REGULATION (EU) 2024/2847 # Article 13 — Obligations of manufacturers > Verbatim text from Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, condensed for readability without altering wording. For the full official text see [eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/2847/oj#art_13). 1. When placing a product with digital elements on the market, manufacturers shall ensure that it has been designed, developed and produced in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements set out in Part I of Annex I and that processes put in place by the manufacturer comply with the essential cybersecurity requirements set out in Part II of Annex I. 2. For the purpose of complying with the obligation laid down in paragraph 1, manufacturers shall undertake an assessment of the cybersecurity risks associated with a product with digital elements and take the outcome of that assessment into account during the planning, design, development, production, delivery and maintenance phases of the product with digital elements with a view to minimising cybersecurity risks, preventing security incidents and minimising the impacts of such incidents, including in relation to the health and safety of users. 3. The cybersecurity risk assessment shall be documented and updated as appropriate during a support period to be determined in accordance with paragraph 8 of this Article. That cybersecurity risk assessment shall comprise at least an analysis of cybersecurity risks based on the intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable use, as well as the conditions of use, of the product with digital elements, such as the operational environment or the assets to be protected, taking into account the length of time the product is expected to be in use. The cybersecurity risk assessment shall indicate whether and, if so in what manner, the security requirements set out in Part I, point (2), of Annex I are applicable to the relevant product with digital elements and how those requirements are implemented as informed by the cybersecurity risk assessment. It shall also indicate how the manufacturer is to apply Part I, point (1), of Annex I and the vulnerability handling requirements set out in Part II of Annex I. 4. When placing a product with digital elements on the market, the manufacturer shall include the cybersecurity risk assessment referred to in paragraph 3 in the technical documentation required pursuant to Article 31 and Annex VII. For products with digital elements referred to in Article 12 that are also subject to other Union legal acts providing for a risk assessment, the cybersecurity risk assessment referred to in paragraph 3 may be part of the risk assessment required by those Union legal acts. 5. Manufacturers shall exercise due diligence when integrating components sourced from third parties so that those components do not compromise the cybersecurity of the product with digital elements, including when integrating components of free and open-source software that have not been made available on the market in the course of a commercial activity. 6. Where a vulnerability has been identified in a component, including in a free and open-source component, which is integrated in the product with digital elements, the manufacturer shall report the vulnerability to the person or entity manufacturing or maintaining the component, and address and remediate the vulnerability in accordance with the vulnerability handling requirements set out in Part II of Annex I. Where manufacturers have developed a software or hardware modification to address the vulnerability in that component, they shall share the relevant code or documentation with the person or entity manufacturing or maintaining the component, where appropriate in a machine-readable format. 7. Manufacturers shall, in a systematic manner, document, in a manner that is proportionate to the nature and to the cybersecurity risks, relevant cybersecurity aspects concerning the product with digital elements, including vulnerabilities of which they become aware and any relevant information provided by third parties, and, where applicable, update the risk assessment of the product. 8. When placing a product with digital elements on the market, manufacturers shall determine the support period, during which manufacturers shall ensure that vulnerabilities of that product are handled effectively and in accordance with the essential cybersecurity requirements set out in Part II of Annex I. The support period shall be commensurate with the period during which the product is expected to be in use, taking into account, in particular, reasonable user expectations, the nature of the product, including its intended purpose, as well as relevant Union law determining the lifetime of products with digital elements. **In determining the support period the manufacturer may also take into account the support periods of products with digital elements offering a similar functionality placed on the market by other manufacturers, the availability of the operating environment, the support periods of integrated components that provide core functions and are sourced from third parties, as well as relevant guidance provided by the dedicated administrative cooperation group (ADCO) established pursuant to Article 52(15) and the Commission. The matters to be taken into account in order to determine the support period shall be considered in a way that ensures proportionality. Without prejudice to the second subparagraph, the support period shall be at least five years. Where the product with digital elements is expected to be in use for less than five years, the support period shall correspond to the expected use time.** 9. Manufacturers shall make available to users the information referred to in Article 13 prior to the purchase of the product with digital elements, and after the placing on the market — throughout the support period — through a clear, intelligible and accessible means. 10–24. *(See EUR-Lex for paragraphs 10 through 24 covering technical documentation, EU declaration of conformity, CE marking, designated points of contact for vulnerability reports, public disclosure of fixed vulnerabilities, retention of records for 10 years

I Essential cybersecurity requirements 21 items II Information and instructions to the user III Important products with digital elements 13 items IV Critical products with digital elements V EU declaration of conformity VI Simplified EU declaration of conformity VII Contents of the technical documentation VIII Conformity assessment procedures ANNEX I Annex I — Essential cybersecurity requirements The substance of conformity — what a product must do and how its maker must handle vulnerabilities. BINDS Manufacturer (Art 13) USED FOR Risk assessment · gap analysis PARTS 13 + 8 items Annex I is the technical heart of the Regulation. It splits into two parts: Part I lists the 13 cybersecurity requirements every product must meet by design (product-level), and Part II lists 8 vulnerability handling process requirements the manufacturer's ORGANISATION must implement (process-level). Article 5 makes both parts mandatory. Annex I §1 Part I — Cybersecurity requirements relating to the properties of products with digital elements 13 product-level requirements. Each applies if the cybersecurity risk assessment (Article 13(2)) shows it is relevant. §1(1) Risk-based design The product must be designed, developed and produced to ensure an appropriate level of cybersecurity based on the risks identified. Implementation — Threat-modelling + cybersecurity risk assessment + design decisions documented in the technical file. §1(2) No known exploitable vulnerabilities at delivery The product must be made available without any known exploitable vulnerabilities. Implementation — Release gate: zero unpatched high/critical CVEs in the SBOM at the moment of placing on the market. §1(3)(a) Configurable for delivery in a secure default configuration The product must be made available with a secure default configuration, including the ability to reset to the original state. Implementation — Factory defaults are secure; documented reset procedure. §1(3)(b) Security update by default Where appropriate to the risk, security updates ensure protection from exploitation, including automatic updates with notification, and the option for the user to opt out. Implementation — Automatic update opt-in by default; user can disable; updates always cryptographically signed. §1(3)(c) Protection from unauthorised access Authentication, identity or access management. Implementation — Authentication on all interfaces; no default credentials; MFA where reasonable for the use case. §1(3)(d) Confidentiality of stored, transmitted and processed data Encryption of relevant data at rest or in transit using state-of-the-art mechanisms. Implementation — TLS 1.3 for transport; AES-256 (or equivalent) for data at rest; documented key management. §1(3)(e) Integrity of data, commands, programs and configuration Integrity protection of stored, transmitted, or processed data against any manipulation or modification not authorised by the user. Implementation — Code signing, signed firmware updates, integrity verification at boundaries, secure boot. §1(3)(f) Data minimisation Only data adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the intended purpose of the product. Implementation — Documented data inventory; collection is opt-in or strictly necessary; retention limits set. §1(3)(g) Availability of essential functions Including resilience and mitigation of denial of service. Implementation — Rate limiting, circuit breakers, graceful degradation, watchdog, monitoring. §1(3)(h) Minimal negative impact on availability of other services Don't be a bad neighbour on the network. Implementation — Bandwidth limits, no broadcast storms, polite DNS / DHCP behaviour. §1(3)(i) Minimise attack surfaces Including limiting external interfaces. Implementation — Remove unused ports/services; close anything not actively required; documented port list. §1(3)(j) Exploit mitigation techniques and reduced impact Reduce impact of incidents using exploit mitigation techniques. Implementation — ASLR, DEP, stack canaries, sandboxing, privilege separation. §1(3)(k) Provide security-relevant information Logging and/or monitoring of relevant internal activity to support incident response and post-incident analysis. Implementation — Security event logging schema; retention; tamper-evident log storage where applicable. §1(3)(l) Secure decommissioning Ability for users to securely remove data and transfer settings when the product is decommissioned or transferred. Implementation — Factory reset that securely wipes data; export configuration to another device. Annex I §2 Part II — Vulnerability handling requirements (process-level) 8 organisational process requirements. These apply to the manufacturer's ENTIRE organisation, not just the product. §2(1) Identify and document vulnerabilities and components Maintain a Software Bill of Materials covering at least the top-level dependencies, in a machine-readable format. Implementation — Automated SBOM generation in CI/CD; CycloneDX 1.5 or SPDX 2.3; published per release. §2(2) Address vulnerabilities without delay Address and remediate vulnerabilities without delay, including by providing security updates. Implementation — Documented patch SLA per severity: critical 7d, high 30d, medium 90d. §2(3) Effective and regular tests Effective security testing and reviews of the product. Implementation — SAST / DAST in CI, dependency scan, annual penetration test, fuzzing for parsing code. §2(4) Public disclosure of fixed vulnerabilities Once a security update has been made available, share and publicly disclose information about fixed vulnerabilities, including a description, allowing users to take corrective actions. Implementation — Security advisory published per fix; CVE reserved; CSAF feed if applicable. §2(5) Coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy Have a policy in place and make available a contact address for receiving information about vulnerabilities. Implementation — Public VDP page + /.well-known/security.txt + dedicated mailbox. ISO/IEC 29147 aligned. §2(6) Facilitate sharing of information about potential vulnerabilities Establish channels to receive vulnerability reports and to inform users about identified vulnerabilities. Implementation — Two-way disclosure channels — receive reports, send advisories. §2(7) Provide secure update mechanisms Provide for mechanisms to securely distribute security updates to ensure that vulnerabilities are fixed in a timely manner and, where applicable for security updates, in an automatic manner. Implementation — Signed updates over authenticated transport; rollback path; automatic by default for consumer products. §2(8) Ensure security update separation Security updates available without delay, free of charge, accompanied by advisory messages, including information on the actions to be taken by users — and (where technically feasible) separated from functionality updates. Implementation — Security-only update channel; advisory text accompanies every security release; users can install security without taking optional functionality. Until the hENs land, the international standards below cover the same ground. Harmonised standards status 41 harmonised standards were requested by the Commission (15 horizontal, 26 vertical). Vulnerability-handling standards target Aug 2026; vertical product standards Oct 2026; all standards Oct 2027. Until then, common specifications (Art 28) may bridge gaps via implementing acts. ISO ISO/IEC 27001 informative Information security management systems ROLE Information Security Management System (ISMS). Covers organisational governance — policies, risk register, role assignment, internal audit. The umbrella, not the product layer (no SBOM or attack-surface minimisation). WHEN TO APPLY Already certified? Use it as evidence for governance, confidentiality and the vulnerability-handling process description in Annex VII. COVERS ▸ Vulnerability handling process Annex I §2(1)-(8) ▸ Risk management Article 13(2)-(4) ▸ Technical documentation alignment Annex VII Find ISO/IEC 27001 ISO ISO/IEC 27034 informative Application security ROLE Application security — secure coding, threat modelling and security review gates at the application layer. WHEN TO APPLY Apply when the product is primarily software. Maps to Annex I Part I (product properties) and Part II §3 (security testing). COVERS ▸ Security by design Annex I §1 ▸ Secure development lifecycle Annex I §2(4) Find ISO/IEC 27034 ISO ISO/IEC 29147 informative Vulnerability disclosure ROLE Vulnerability disclosure — how an organisation receives reports from external researchers: policy, contact mailbox, acknowledgement, coordinated timelines. WHEN TO APPLY Required input for Annex I Part II §5. Author your CVD policy against ISO 29147. COVERS ▸ Coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy Annex I §2(5), Article 13(8) Find ISO/IEC 29147 ISO ISO/IEC 30111 informative Vulnerability handling processes ROLE Vulnerability handling — the internal process to receive, triage, remediate and disclose. The internal complement to ISO 29147. WHEN TO APPLY Required input for Annex I Part II §1–§8. Author your vulnerability-handling procedures against ISO 30111. COVERS ▸ Internal vulnerability handling Annex I §2(1)-(8) Find ISO/IEC 30111 IEC IEC 62443-4-1 candidate Secure product development lifecycle requirements ROLE Secure product development lifecycle for industrial components — SDLC, threat modelling, security requirements, testing, update mechanisms. WHEN TO APPLY Apply for industrial / IACS-adjacent products, or as a security-by-design framework likely to become a harmonised standard. COVERS ▸ Security by design Annex I §1 ▸ Security testing evidence Annex VII §6 Find IEC 62443-4-1 IEC IEC 62443-4-2 candidate Technical security requirements for IACS components ROLE Technical security requirements for IACS components — authentication, confidentiality, integrity, audit, malware protection. Pairs with 4-1 (process → technical). WHEN TO APPLY Apply alongside 4-1 for industrial products. Maps to Annex I Part I item-by-item. COVERS ▸ Essential cybersecurity requirements Annex I §1 Find IEC 62443-4-2 ENISA ENISA Vulnerability Handling Guidelines informative Operational guidance for vulnerability handling and SRP submission ROLE ENISA's operational guidance on vulnerability handling and SRP submission — less normative than ISO, more 'how to actually do it'. WHEN TO APPLY Reference when defining the 24h / 72h / 14d submission runbook — it describes what ENISA expects in each SRP phase. visibleText: D Product Security OS DestroSolutions Home Products Friday Inbox Chats Projects Run history Security Vulnerabilities Threat intel PSIRT Supply chain Compliance Workspace Reports Integrations Settings Search products, CVEs, playbooks… Ctrl K SS Singh Admin LEARN Overview Documents OPERATE SBOM Builder License risk Container scan Destro Gate Renovate bridge Early signals OSS steward REFERENCE Articles (71) Annexes (8) Standards Timeline RASIC Open source ENISA SRP Compliance dashboard REFERENCE · OPEN SOURCE UNDER THE CRA Steward vs volunteer Article 24 creates the open-source software steward — a legal person (not an individual) that sustainedly supports FOSS used commercially. Light-touch obligations. Individual contributors stay outside scope (Recital 18). Three-question decision Q1 Is the entity supporting the FOSS a legal person (foundation, association, company)? Individual maintainers are not legal persons here. A hobby project, a thesis, one person on GitHub — out. Q2 Does it systematically support development on a sustained basis? Infrastructure, governance, release management, security policies — not one-off contributions. Q3 Is the FOSS used by third parties for commercial activity? Used in commercial products / services downstream. The FOSS itself need not be sold. ALL THREE YES Steward — in scope Article 24 obligations apply (light-touch). ANY ANSWER NO Volunteer — out of scope Recital 18 — fully exempt. OSS steward IN SCOPE A legal person, other than a manufacturer, that systematically and on a sustained basis supports the development of specific FOSS products with digital elements intended for commercial activity, and ensures their viability. OBLIGATIONS ▸ Adopt and document a cybersecurity policy for secure development and vulnerability handling — Art 24(1). ▸ Cooperate with market surveillance authorities — Art 24(2). ▸ Report actively-exploited vulnerabilities and severe incidents via the ENISA SRP — Art 24(3) → 14. ▸ Provide reasonable assistance to manufacturers integrating the FOSS — Art 25. EXEMPTIONS ▸ Not subject to administrative fines — Art 64(10), even where obligations apply. ▸ No notified-body assessment for the steward role. ▸ No steward-level technical file — the upstream code documents itself. Article 24 on EUR-Lex OSS volunteer / contributor EXEMPT An individual contributor who develops or contributes to FOSS outside the course of a commercial activity. Explicitly outside CRA scope (Recital 18). OBLIGATIONS None. Recital 18 places non-commercial individual contributors fully outside CRA scope — free to develop, publish, fork and contribute as the ecosystem always has. REASONABLE EXPECTATIONS Continue good security practice voluntarily — sensible craft, not a CRA obligation. Recital 18 on EUR-Lex Worked examples Linux Foundation Hosts the Linux kernel + 800+ projects used commercially worldwide. STEWARD Apache Software Foundation Hosts Apache HTTP Server, Kafka, Tomcat, Spark — many in commercial products. STEWARD Eclipse Foundation Hosts Jakarta EE, Eclipse IDE — used commercially across automotive and industrial. STEWARD OpenSSL Software Foundation Sustains OpenSSL — embedded in nearly every product with TLS. STEWARD Individual maintainer of a hobby package Single developer, ad-hoc commits, no commercial sustaining. VOLUNTEER Student publishing a thesis project Personal academic work, no commercial intent. VOLUNTEER If you integrate FOSS as a component Article 25 obligates the manufacturer — not the steward or the volunteer — when integrating FOSS components: ▸ Exercise due diligence — verify the FOSS doesn't compromise the product's cybersecurity (Art 13(5)). ▸ Report identified vulnerabilities in the FOSS back to the upstream maintainer or steward. ▸ Share fixes you developed for the FOSS where appropriate, in machine-readable format. ▸ Include the FOSS components in your SBOM at top level. © 2026 DestroSolutions Friday Good afternoon, Singh. ⊟ 6 exploited CVEs are open. visibleText: D Product Security OS DestroSolutions Home Products Friday Inbox Chats Projects Run history Security Vulnerabilities Threat intel PSIRT Supply chain Compliance Workspace Reports Integrations Settings Search products, CVEs, playbooks… Ctrl K SS Singh Admin LEARN Overview Documents OPERATE SBOM Builder License risk Container scan Destro Gate Renovate bridge Early signals OSS steward REFERENCE Articles (71) Annexes (8) Standards Timeline RASIC Open source ENISA SRP Compliance dashboard REFERENCE · SINGLE REPORTING PLATFORM ENISA SRP — submission brief The EU-level gate to notify ENISA + the coordinator CSIRT of actively-exploited vulnerabilities (Art 14) and severe incidents (Art 22) — one submission auto-routes to both. Mandatory from 11 September 2026. Launch status Reporting under Article 14 has been mandatory since 11 September 2026 (Art 71(2)). The SRP is a web form — there is no public API, so every notification is submitted by hand on the ENISA platform. Destro prepares the submission; it does not file it for you. ENISA SRP official page Why the SRP matters ▸ One submission, two recipients — ENISA and your coordinator CSIRT receive it simultaneously. ▸ The coordinator CSIRT (Member State of main establishment, Art 14(7)) disseminates to other CSIRTs. ▸ Uniform schema across all Member States — same fields, same phases, same SLAs. Vulnerability Severe incident Deadlines from the moment of awareness 1. 24 hours Awareness of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident Article 14(1)(a) 2. 72 hours Preliminary notification — general info + initial assessment Article 14(1)(b) / 22(1)(b) 3. 14 days Final report — vulnerability (after corrective measure available) Article 14(1)(c) Submission fields · vulnerability FIELD PHASE REQUIREMENT DESCRIPTION Notification type 24h REQUIRED Vulnerability or Incident. Notification level 24h REQUIRED 24h / 72h / Final. Reporter identity 24h REQUIRED Legal entity submitting. Manufacturer / OSS Steward name 24h REQUIRED Entity behind the affected product. Product name 24h REQUIRED Commercial product name. Product type 24h REQUIRED Default / Important / Critical. Member States where available 24h REQUIRED Markets affected. Title 24h REQUIRED Brief headline. CVE ID 24h OPTIONAL Carried forward to later phases. EUVD ID 24h OPTIONAL ENISA EU Vulnerability Database ID. General nature of vulnerability / exploit 72h REQUIRED What it is and how it's being exploited. Corrective / mitigating measures taken 72h REQUIRED What you've done so far. User-actionable mitigations 72h REQUIRED What users can do today. Severity assessment Final REQUIRED CVSS-style severity with reasoning. Impact statement Final REQUIRED Real-world consequences. Malicious actor details 72h IF KNOWN Identified threat actor, if known. Security update details Final REQUIRED Patch version, channel, deployment guidance. Routing — one submission, two recipients 1 Manufacturer OR OSS STEWARD Moment of awareness triggers the SLA clock. 2 ENISA SRP WEB FORM One submission with the fields required for the phase. 3 ENISA + coordinator CSIRT SIMULTANEOUS Coordinator = your main-establishment Member State (Art 14(7)). 4 Other CSIRTs DISSEMINATED Unless an Art 16(2) exceptional-circumstances delay applies. "Moment of awareness" — the trigger The 24-hour clock starts when the manufacturer has reliable evidence that the vulnerability is being exploited or the incident is occurring. Internal triage delays do not stop the clock. Practical implication: detection must produce a timestamp and transition to incident response within minutes. The 24h, 72h and 14d phases are calculated from that timestamp. © 2026 DestroSolutions Friday Good afternoon, Singh. ⊟ 6 exploited CVEs are open. Start with CVE-2016-5195. from last placement on the market (Article 13(15)) destrosolutions.com 3 CRA · Article 33 + Annex VII Technical Documentation (Annex VII) 1 General product description 1.1 Product purpose ECU-X42 Domain Controller is a product with digital elements supplied by DestroSolutions GmbH for the EU market. Its intended purpose, intended users, essential functionality and operating environment are recorded here and in the accompanying user information (Annex II). TO COMPLETE State the product's specific intended purpose in 1–2 sentences. 1.2 Reasonably foreseeable use The risk assessment in Section 3 considers reasonably foreseeable use beyond the intended purpose, including the misuse scenarios the design defends against. TO COMPLETE Summarise the principal foreseeable-misuse scenarios for this product. 1.3 Product type and classification • Tier (Default / Important Class I / Important Class II / Critical): tier • Annex III / IV reference (if applicable): ref • Conformity assessment module applied: Module module 1.4 Product identifiers • Brand name: DestroSolutions GmbH • Model number(s): model numbers • Serial number scheme: serial scheme • Hardware revisions covered: hw revs • Firmware / software versions covered: fw versions destrosolutions.com 4 CRA · Article 33 + Annex VII Technical Documentation (Annex VII) 2 Design, development and production 2.1 Architecture overview The product architecture, trust boundaries, external interfaces, data flows and third-party components are documented in the architecture record. Trust boundaries are enforced at every external interface, and all inbound data crossing a boundary is authenticated and validated before processing. TO COMPLETE Attach the current architecture diagram for this release. 2.2 Secure development lifecycle The product is developed under a secure development lifecycle aligned to IEC 62443-4-1, with mandatory security gates at: • Requirements review • Architecture and threat-model sign-off • Implementation review with static analysis (SAST) • Pre-release dynamic testing (DAST, fuzzing, penetration test) • Documented release sign-off Security defects are tracked to closure before release. 2.3 Cybersecurity design decisions Significant security design decisions — the alternatives considered, the risk each mitigates or accepts, and the rationale — are recorded in the design-decision log. TO COMPLETE Reference the design-decision log for this release. destrosolutions.com 5 CRA · Article 33 + Annex VII Technical Documentation (Annex VII) 3 Cybersecurity risk assessment (Article 13(2)-(4)) 3.1 Assets and protection objectives The assets the product protects, their confidentiality / integrity / availability objectives and their data classifications are inventoried in the risk assessment. TO COMPLETE List the principal assets and data types this product processes. 3.2 Threat model A STRIDE-based threat model identifies trust boundaries, attacker capabilities and attack vectors, with a documented rationale and disposition for each threat. TO COMPLETE Reference or attach the current threat model. 3.3 Risk scoring • Methodology: DestroSolutions Risk Calculator (Article 13(2)), cross-referenced to ISO/IEC 27005 • Score: score / 100 • Tier: risk tier • Date of last assessment: assessment date 3.4 Risk treatment Each identified risk carries a documented treatment (reduce / accept), the residual-risk decision, the accountable owner and the verification method. Risks rated High or Critical are reduced before placing on the market; any accepted residual risk is signed off at senior level under Article 13(3). attach the risk-treatment register. destrosolutions.com 6 CRA · Article 33 + Annex VII Technical Documentation (Annex VII) 4 Essential cybersecurity requirements (Annex I Part I) A point-by-point demonstration of conformity with each applicable requirement of Annex I Part I. Requirements assessed as not applicable are justified in writing under Article 13(4). 4.1 No known exploitable vulnerabilities — §2(a) Measure Verified at release through static application security testing (SAST), software composition analysis against the SBOM, and manual review of security-critical code. No vulnerability rated CVSS ≥ 7.0 is open at the point of placing on the market. Evidence release scan report + sign-off record 4.2 Secure-by-default configuration — §2(b) Measure The product ships in a hardened default configuration with no default or hard-coded credentials. Unused services and interfaces are disabled by default, and the user can reset the product to its secure original state. Evidence configuration baseline document 4.3 Confidentiality of data — §2(e) Measure Data at rest and in transit is protected with state-of-the-art cryptography (TLS 1.2+ in transit; AES-256 at rest). Keys are handled under the documented key-management procedure. Evidence cryptography spec + key-management policy 4.4 Integrity — §2(f) Measure Integrity of stored data, commands and configuration is protected through signed firmware, secure boot and integrity verification at trust boundaries; corruption is detected and reported. Evidence secure-boot and signing design 4.5 Availability — §2(h) Measure Essential and basic functions remain available under load; rate-limiting and resource controls provide resilience to denial-of-service. Evidence availability / dos test results 4.6 Data minimisation — §2(g) Measure Only data adequate, relevant and limited to the intended purpose is processed; each data element and its purpose are recorded in the data inventory. Evidence data inventory 4.7 Access control — §2(d) Measure Access requires authentication; authorisation follows least privilege; sessions are managed and protected. Unauthorised-access attempts are logged and can be reported. Evidence identity & access management design 4.8 Attack-surface minimisation — §2(j) Measure External interfaces, ports and services are inventoried and minimised; the resulting attack surface is recorded in the hardening guide. Evidence port/service inventory + hardening guide 4.9 Exploitation-mitigation techniques — §2(k) Measure The build enables exploitation-mitigation techniques (ASLR, DEP/NX, stack protection) and, where applicable, component sandboxing, to limit the impact of any exploited vulnerability. Evidence build configuration record 4.10 Security logging — §2(l) Measure Security-relevant events are logged to a documented schema with defined retention; logging can be disabled by the user where required. Evidence logging schema 4.11 Secure data removal — §2(m) Measure The user can securely and permanently remove all data and settings, and transfer them to another product where supported. Evidence secure-erase procedure 4.12 Security updates — §2(c) Measure Security updates are delivered over a secure, signed channel with a rollback path, automatic by default with a user opt-out, and free of charge for the support period. visibleText: D Product Security OS DestroSolutions Home Products Friday Inbox Chats Projects Run history Security Vulnerabilities Threat intel PSIRT Supply chain Compliance Workspace Reports Integrations Settings Search products, CVEs, playbooks… Ctrl K SS Singh Admin HELP Docs Getting started Formats API reference Getting started 1 Create your account Sign up with your work email. You become the owner of a new organization. Sign up 2 Add a product Products → Register product. One product per ECU, device or software release line. Open Products 3 Upload an SBOM or firmware On the product page, upload a CycloneDX or SPDX JSON SBOM. For a binary image, use Firmware uploads to extract one. CI pipelines can upload through the API. Open Firmware uploads 4 Review findings Components are matched against known vulnerabilities. Open Vulnerabilities, or the product's Vulnerabilities tab, and click a finding for details. Open Vulnerabilities 5 Record VEX decisions In a finding, set its VEX status: affected, not affected, fixed or under investigation. A 'not affected' decision needs a justification before it is exported. Open Vulnerabilities 6 Export On the product's Vulnerabilities tab, Export gives STIX 2.1, CSAF 2.0 VEX or OpenVEX. The API also exports the SBOM as CycloneDX. Open Products 7 Run PSIRT cases Open and track product security incidents and advisories in PSIRT. Open PSIRT Formats Format Import Export CycloneDX JSON (SBOM) Product SBOM upload · API upload API: CycloneDX 1.5 SPDX 2.x JSON (SBOM) Product SBOM upload · API upload Not available CSAF 2.0 VEX API VEX import Product Export menu · API OpenVEX 0.2.0 API VEX import Product Export menu · API CycloneDX VEX API VEX import Not available STIX 2.1 Threat feeds → STIX bundle import Product Export menu TAXII 2.1 Not available TAXII server for KEV and advisories (client tokens under Threat feeds) API reference Base URL: https://iaxxugiyicroptkuhgyj.supabase.co/functions/v1/api-gateway Authentication: header X-API-Key with a key from Integrations → API keys. Every request is scoped to the organization that owns the API key. Create a key under Integrations → API keys. The key is shown once; only its SHA-256 hash is stored. Scopes: `read` (products, findings, scans, exports), `upload` (SBOM upload, creates the product version if it is new), `write` (VEX import, webhook test event). A signed-in user's session token is accepted for `read` routes only. Limits: 60 requests per minute and 10,000 per day per key. Over the limit the API answers `429` with a `Retry-After` header. Request bodies are limited to 20 MB. Every response (except exports, which return the document itself) uses the envelope `{ data, meta: { request_id, took_ms, pagination? }, errors: [] }`. CI/CD quick start · OpenAPI v1 file: docs/api/openapi.yaml Health GET /api/v1/health no key Check the API is up Responses: 200 Products GET /api/v1/products scope: read List products page? query integer per_page? query integer Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 403 · 429 GET /api/v1/products/{id} scope: read Get one product id path string (uuid) Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 Findings GET /api/v1/products/{id}/findings scope: read List a product's findings id path string (uuid) severity? query critical | high | medium | low | info kev? query true | false Only findings that are (true) or are not (false) in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. page? query integer per_page? query integer Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 GET /api/v1/findings scope: read List findings across all products product_id? query string (uuid) severity? query critical | high | medium | low | info kev? query true | false Only findings that are (true) or are not (false) in CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list. page? query integer per_page? query integer Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 429 GET /api/v1/findings/{id} scope: read Get one finding id path string (uuid) Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 SBOM GET /api/v1/products/{id}/sbom scope: read List a product's components id path string (uuid) Responses: 200 · 401 · 404 · 429 POST /api/v1/sbom/upload scope: upload Upload a CycloneDX or SPDX JSON SBOM to a product version Send either an envelope, or the SBOM itself as the body with the product named in the query string. A product named by `product_name` + `product_version` that does not exist yet is created. The upload is accepted (202) and matched against vulnerabilities in the background; poll `GET /api/v1/scans/{import_id}` until `finished` is true. Uploading the same SBOM again returns the existing scan (`duplicate: true`). product_id? query string (uuid) Used when the body is the raw SBOM. product_name? query string Used when the body is the raw SBOM. product_version? query string Used when the body is the raw SBOM. Required to create a new product version. file_name? query string Takes a JSON body. Responses: 202 · 400 · 401 · 403 · 404 · 409 · 413 · 422 · 429 GET /api/v1/scans/{id} scope: read Get the status of an SBOM upload id path string (uuid) The `import_id` returned by the upload. Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 Exports GET /api/v1/products/{id}/export/cyclonedx scope: read Export the product SBOM as CycloneDX 1.5 JSON id path string (uuid) Responses: 200 · 401 · 404 · 409 · 422 · 429 GET /api/v1/products/{id}/export/vex scope: read Export the product's VEX as OpenVEX 0.2.0 or CSAF 2.0 A finding marked not affected with no recorded justification is left out rather than asserted; `X-Omitted-Statements` says how many. CSAF needs the organization's website or domain for the publisher namespace and is refused (422) without one. id path string (uuid) format? query openvex | csaf Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 422 · 429 Policy GET /api/v1/products/{id}/policy scope: read Evaluate the organization's release policy for a product Evaluates the policy saved for the organization (Integrations → Policy). When none is saved, the default policy is used and `policy.source` is `default`. A fact that could not be read makes its rule `not_checked`; `verdict` is `fail` if any rule fails, else `not_checked` if any rule could not be checked, else `pass`. id path string (uuid) Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 POST /api/v1/products/{id}/policy/evaluate scope: read Evaluate a policy document (policy as code) for a product Send the policy kept in your repository (psoc-policy.json), either as the body or as `{ "policy": {...} }`. Nothing is stored. Schema: integrations/ci/psoc-policy.schema.json. id path string (uuid) Takes a JSON body. Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 PSIRT GET /api/v1/psirt/cases scope: read List PSIRT cases status? query string severity? query string page? query integer per_page? query integer Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 429 VEX POST /api/v1/vex/import scope: write Import supplier VEX documents Each statement is stored and processed in the background (OpenVEX, CycloneDX VEX or CSAF VEX). Poll `GET /api/v1/jobs/{id}` for each job id. Takes a JSON body. Responses: 202 · 400 · 401 · 403 · 429 Jobs GET /api/v1/jobs/{id} scope: read Get the status of a background job id path integer Responses: 200 · 400 · 401 · 404 · 429 Webhooks POST /api/v1/webhooks/test scope: write Queue a test event for one of your webhooks Takes a JSON body. Responses: 202 · 400 · 401 · 403 · 404 · 429 © 2026 DestroSolutions Friday Good afternoon, Singh. ⊟ 6 exploited CVEs are open. Start with CVE-2016-5195. Confirm exposure on the affected product Open Products → the affected product → Vulnerabilities. Confirm the CVE row is present and tagged KEV. Detect · Security analyst 2. Open a PSIRT case PSIRT → Cases → New case. Severity = critical. Source = internal_scan. Link the CVE id. Investigate · PSIRT lead 3. Notify customer-facing channels Post to #cs-security and #sales-eng. Use the standard KEV alert template. Communicate · PSIRT comms 4. Apply mitigation or shutdown Patch path on the CVE drawer. If patch can't ship in 24h, evaluate WAF rule or feature-flag shutdown. If yes: Patch shipped → step 5. If no: Shutdown path → step 5 (with note). Remediate · Engineering 5. Draft and publish a customer advisory Promote the case to an advisory. Set status to in_review, get sign-off, publish. Communicate · PSIRT lead 6. Post-mortem within 5 business days Document what we caught, what we missed, and the auto-detect we'll add for next time.
